1.title: Choose crops, space and a first customer
1.intro: Vertical gardens grow food or plants in stacked layers indoors or on walls. They suit places with little land and high prices for fresh produce.
pts: Compare crops by days to harvest, price per kilogram and light needed: leafy greens and herbs turn fastest; fruit crops need more space and light.
Find a first customer within an hour's drive: restaurants, grocers, food programmes, office tenants who want green walls.
Ask each for weekly volume, price they pay now and the freshness gap you can close.
Write the offer: 'fresh [crop], harvested the day before, delivered twice a week at [price] per kilogram'.
1.ex: Basil sells at 28 per kilogram to restaurants who now pay 36 for imported. Demand: 12 kg per week across three kitchens.
1.act: Interview five buyers and fill a crop table with price, volume and delivery frequency.
1.std: Five buyers recorded; one crop chosen with reasons.

2.title: Know the rules for growing and selling in Canada
2.intro: Growing under lights is farming, manufacturing and a building project at once.
pts: Food grown for sale follows federal food-safety and labelling rules; the local public health unit may inspect washing and packing areas.
Building and fire rules apply to racks, wiring and water; get electrical work done by licensed trades and inspected.
Water use, nutrient discharge and waste are regulated by the municipality and province.
Insurance for crop loss, equipment and liability should be arranged before the first harvest.
2.ex: Row: 'Pack leafy greens for sale | food inspection agency and local health unit | register and follow wash and pack rules | before first sale | inspection report'.
2.act: Make the rules table for a rented warehouse unit in your province.
2.std: Each row cites an official source and date.

3.title: Design the system and grow a first crop
3.intro: Good vertical growing is a controlled loop: light, water, nutrients, air and time.
pts: Choose a system: hydroponic (roots in water), aeroponic (roots misted) or soil-based wall.
Set targets: light hours per day, nutrient strength (conductivity), water pH, temperature and humidity.
Log these daily; change one setting at a time.
Track yield per tray per cycle and days to harvest.
3.ex: Lettuce: 28 days to harvest, 0.45 kg per tray, 12 trays per rack, 10 racks: 54 kg per cycle.
3.act: Grow one tray cycle; log daily readings and final yield.
3.std: Daily log complete; yield per tray calculated.

4.title: Cost it: power, labour and trays
4.intro: Electricity for lights is usually the largest cost after rent.
pts: Power cost per cycle = lamp kilowatts x hours per day x days x price per kWh.
Add labour for seeding, moving, harvesting and cleaning.
Compute cost per tray and per kilogram; compare with selling price.
Test a 10% power price rise and a 15% yield drop.
4.ex: Per tray: power 14, seeds and nutrients 6, packaging 4, labour 14 = 38 variable; price 95 per tray-equivalent; margin 57 (60%). Break-even about 380 trays a month with fixed cost 21,700. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build the cost sheet for your system and compute break-even.

5.title: Run clean, steady operations
5.intro: Hygiene, schedules and records keep crops safe and predictable.
pts: Clean trays and tanks between cycles; sanitise tools; wash hands at entry.
Stagger seeding weekly so harvests are steady.
Scout for pests and mould twice a week; remove problem trays at once.
Keep a harvest and delivery log with batch numbers for traceability.
5.ex: Batch code 'B-0417-T3' links a delivered bag to the tray, seed lot and cleaning record.
5.act: Keep a 4-week operations log with batch numbers.
5.std: Every delivery traces back to a tray.

6.title: Sell, deliver and keep the customer
6.intro: Restaurants and grocers value a steady supply and a person who answers.
pts: Offer a standing weekly order with a trial week.
Deliver on a fixed day and time; confirm by message the day before.
Tell the story: seed to harvest dates, no spray, local.
Ask for feedback after four weeks and adjust crop mix.
6.ex: Funnel: 15 visits, 6 samples, 3 trial orders, 2 standing orders.
6.act: Visit ten buyers with samples and record outcomes.

7.title: Manage food safety and power risks
7.intro: A power cut or contamination can end a crop in hours.
pts: List risks: power failure, pump failure, contamination, pest, buyer loss.
Controls: backup power for pumps, alarms, spare parts, test water.
Recall plan: know which batches went where and how to tell buyers.
Energy plan: efficient lamps, off-peak hours, rooftop or contract renewable power.
7.ex: Risk: 'Pump fails overnight | 2 x 5 | float alarm and spare pump | owner | monthly test'.
7.std: Each row has owner and test date.

8.title: Pilot one room and plan growth
8.intro: Prove one room before you build ten.
pts: Pilot 60 days with measures: yield, cost per kilogram, orders kept.
Stop rule: below 60% of planned yield after two cycles, pause and fix.
Scale in steps: second room only after margin holds.
Plan funding: grants for local food and clean technology, and customer pre-orders.
8.ex: Result at day 60: 48 kg per cycle against 54 plan (89%); proceed.
8.act: Run the pilot and present review.

quiz: Why compare crops by days to harvest?
Faster crops return cash sooner and fit stacked systems best.
What is usually the largest cost after rent?
Electricity for lights.
How do you compute power cost per cycle?
Lamp kilowatts x hours per day x days x price per kWh.
Why use batch codes?
They trace a delivered bag back to its tray and enable recalls.
Name three growing systems.
Hydroponic, aeroponic and soil-based wall.
What should a risk register include for pumps?
A control such as an alarm and a spare, an owner and a test date.
What is a stop rule in the pilot?
A pre-agreed trigger, such as yield under 60% of plan, to pause and fix.
Why stagger seeding?
Harvests stay steady week to week.
Who inspects wash and pack areas?
The local public health unit may inspect them.
Why test a 15% yield drop?
It shows whether the business still breaks even under stress.
